title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure
vars <- load_variables(2023, "acs5")
View(vars)
Then use the search box. :::

my_state <- "CO"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25077_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 64  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                       variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                      <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 08001 Adams County, Colorado     B25077_001   458400  3021
2 08003 Alamosa County, Colorado   B25077_001   218800 21223
3 08005 Arapahoe County, Colorado  B25077_001   526000  5958
4 08007 Archuleta County, Colorado B25077_001   451400 16410
5 08009 Baca County, Colorado      B25077_001   122000 22458
6 08011 Bent County, Colorado      B25077_001   137900 26527


There are 64 counties in Colorado and that number matches the rows returned by dim(country_data) which is 5.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe/estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate    moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Jackson County, Colorado      250000 104968    42.0
 2 San Miguel County, Colorado   613100 165694    27.0
 3 San Juan County, Colorado     406900  93791    23.1
 4 Kiowa County, Colorado        148600  30604    20.6
 5 Bent County, Colorado         137900  26527    19.2
 6 Baca County, Colorado         122000  22458    18.4
 7 Lake County, Colorado         401300  67434    16.8
 8 Cheyenne County, Colorado     187100  31159    16.7
 9 Saguache County, Colorado     200000  30566    15.3
10 Huerfano County, Colorado     256700  37763    14.7


Jackson County, Colorado has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate.Jackson County’s ACS median home-value estimate has a margin of error equal to about 42% of the estimate, making it the least precise estimate in the displayed set.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    23
2 Low confidence     21
3 Moderate           20


I evaluated the reliability of ACS estimates for median owner-occupied home values across Colorado counties by calculating each estimate’s margin of error as a percentage of its reported value: (MOE/estimate)×100.Counties with a relative MOE below 5% were classified as high confidence, those between 5% and 10% as moderate confidence, and those above 10% as low confidence. These thresholds are interpretive rather than official Census reliability standards, but they create a useful distribution for this county-level analysis: 23 counties have high-confidence estimates, 20 have moderately reliable estimates, and 21 have low-confidence estimates.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                       myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 08001 Adams County, Colorado     458400   3021 524408    NA
2 08003 Alamosa County, Colorado   218800  21223  16515    NA
3 08005 Arapahoe County, Colorado  526000   5958 655709    NA
4 08007 Archuleta County, Colorado 451400  16410  13730    NA
5 08009 Baca County, Colorado      122000  22458   3460    NA
6 08011 Bent County, Colorado      137900  26527   5524    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         23        234182.
2 Low confidence           9          4015.
3 Moderate                32         12139.


High-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 234,182 people, compared with about 4,015 people in low-confidence counties. Moderate-reliability counties have an average population of approximately 12,139 people. This pattern suggests that, in this dataset, more populous counties generally have more precise ACS median home-value estimates, while less populous counties tend to have larger relative margins of error and lower-confidence estimates.

section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6

  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 08001 Adams County, Colorado     458400   3021 524408    NA
2 08003 Alamosa County, Colorado   218800  21223  16515    NA
3 08005 Arapahoe County, Colorado  526000   5958 655709    NA
4 08007 Archuleta County, Colorado 451400  16410  13730    NA
5 08009 Baca County, Colorado      122000  22458   3460    NA
6 08011 Bent County, Colorado      137900  26527   5524    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         23        234182.
2 Low confidence           9          4015.
3 Moderate                32         12139.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]
High-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 234,182 people, compared with about 4,015 people in low-confidence counties. Moderate-reliability counties have an average population of approximately 12,139 people. This pattern suggests that, in this dataset, more populous counties generally have more precise ACS median home-value estimates, while less populous counties tend to have larger relative margins of error and lower-confidence estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Colorado communities with the least reliable ACS estimates of median owner-occupied home values are primarily small, rural counties. Jackson County has the greatest uncertainty: its estimated median home value is $250,000, with a margin of error of ±$104,968, or 42.0% of the estimate. Other counties with relatively high uncertainty include San Miguel County (27.0%), San Juan County (23.1%), Kiowa County (20.6%), Bent County (19.2%), and Baca County (18.4%). Using the selected thresholds, nine counties fall into the low-confidence category, compared with 23 high-confidence and 32 moderate-reliability counties.
This pattern reflects how the American Community Survey (ACS) works. Unlike a complete census count, the ACS is a continuous sample survey. Its estimates are based on responses from a subset of households rather than every household. Smaller counties contain fewer households and therefore tend to produce smaller survey samples. Smaller samples create more sampling variability, which appears as a larger margin of error relative to the reported estimate. ACS sampling error is generally lower when the sample size is larger, while small-area estimates often require pooled multi-year data to achieve usable precision.
A state agency that allocates housing assistance, property-tax relief, or infrastructure funding based on median home values—but treats every county estimate as equally precise—could make poorly targeted decisions. Rural, low-population counties would be most vulnerable. For example, Jackson County could be classified as comparatively high-value or low-value based on an estimate with a confidence interval spanning roughly $145,032 to $354,968. Funding formulas that ignore this uncertainty could underfund communities with genuine housing need or direct funds away from them based on unstable measurements. Agencies should therefore incorporate MOEs, confidence intervals, or reliability flags when comparing counties and making resource-allocation decision.
Reflections
When assessing estimates of median owner-occupied home values, it is important to consider margins of error and confidence intervals, as these measures provide greater context for informed policy-making. Relying solely on arbitrary or point estimates may lead to misleading conclusions and ineffective policy decisions. Counties seeking to implement policies that produce meaningful change should therefore account for the uncertainty surrounding these estimates when evaluating housing conditions and allocating resources.

section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more






NoteDelete this box



None of these are graded. There are no extra points. A complete, well-written assignment earns a 2 either way.
They’re here for anyone who finished the above and found it straightforward. Pick one (or more) that interests you.

Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.
Parameterize the report. Add params: to the YAML so the state is an input rather than hard-coded, and the same file regenerates for any state. Render it from the terminal with quarto render assignment2.qmd -P state:NY.
Write a function and iterate. Wrap the data pull in a function, then use purrr::map_dfr() to run it across several states at once. Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?
Change the geographic scale. Run the same variable at geography = "tract" inside one county. Compare the margins of error to what you saw at county level. What does that imply about the resolution at which you can actually trust ACS data?

If you try one, add a short section describing what you did and what you found.

7. R Is Case Sensitive
counties ≠ Counties; moe_pct ≠ MOE_pct. Always match exact spelling/capitalization.

title: Week 2: dplyr and census
text:
8. Census Data

Decennial Census: every 10 years, full population count.
ACS (American Community Survey): sample-based (since 2005), gives detailed demographic/economic/housing data plus a margin of error (MOE) since it’s an estimate, not a full count.

title: Week 2: dplyr and census
text:
9. ACS Data Products

1-Year estimates: larger areas/populations only.
5-Year estimates: smaller areas (tracts, block groups, counties, places); e.g. a 2023 5-year estimate covers the 5-year period ending 2023.

title: Week 2: dplyr and census
text:
10. Estimates and Margins of Error
Every ACS value pairs an estimate with an MOE indicating uncertainty:



County
Income

Always report/interpret estimates alongside their MOE.

title: Week 2: dplyr and census
text:
11. Census Variable IDs
B19013_001E → B(base table) 19013(table number) 001(line number) E(estimate). The MOE version ends in M (B19013_001M).

title: Week 2: dplyr and census
text:
12. Geography in Census Data
Hierarchy: State → County → Census Tract → Block Group → Block. Not all datasets cover every level. Tract boundaries can shift over time — use NHGIS or LTDB/LTDR for longitudinal comparisons.

title: Week 2: dplyr and census
text:
13. Blocks and Block Groups
Blocks are the smallest unit (Decennial only, little ACS data). Block groups (collections of blocks) allow detailed analysis but often carry large MOEs due to small sample sizes.

title: Week 2: dplyr and census
text:
14. GEOIDs
Unique geographic identifier, e.g. 42101000100 = 42(PA) + 101(county) + 000100(tract). Used to join Census data to boundary files.

title: Week 2: dplyr and census
text:
17. Key Concepts to Remember

Console = testing; R script = saved code; Quarto chunk = code inside .qmd.
Objects store data; functions act on objects; arguments guide functions.
filter() rows, select() columns, mutate() new/modified columns, arrange() order, group_by()/summarize() grouped stats.
Pipes (|>/%>%) chain steps; R is case sensitive.
ACS = estimates with MOE, not exact counts; GEOIDs identify geography; geography can change over time.
tidycensus fetches Census/ACS data; results can be long or wide format.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
1. YAML
YAML is the configuration block at the top of a .qmd file. It begins and ends with three dashes:
---
title: "My Portfolio"
author: "Emmanuel Sampson"
date: today
format: html
---
YAML can specify:

The title and author
The date
Output format, such as HTML
Table of contents settings
Whether code is shown or hidden
Other document-level options


Important YAML Rules

Indentation matters.
Use spaces, not tabs.
A colon must have a space after it:

title: "My Page"

YAML begins at the first line of the document.
The opening and closing --- lines must both be present.

A common error is incorrect indentation.
For example, this is wrong:
website:
navbar:
  title: "Portfolio"
Because navbar should be nested under website.
The correct version is:
website:
  navbar:
    title: "Portfolio"

title: About Me
text:
About Me
I am a geospatial professional and graduate student in Urban Spatial Analytics at the University of Pennsylvania. My work brings together spatial data science, GIS, surveying and mapping technology, and commercial strategy.
I have experience in geospatial business development, strategic account management, and partnership development. My interests include GNSS, aerial mapping, optical monitoring, remote sensing, and the use of spatial data to support better urban and infrastructure decisions.
This portfolio documents my work in public-policy analytics and urban spatial analysis. It includes projects that use GIS, spatial statistics, data visualization, and reproducible analytical workflows to explore real-world questions.
